docs.text: inspy-conv ¶ inspy-conv is a Python toolkit for inelastic neutron scattering data analysis: triple-axis spectrometer resolution calculation , resolution-convolution fitting , crystallography helpers, and Qt GUIs . Install name: inspy-conv — import name: inspy Version: 0.3.5 — Python ≥ 3.8 — MIT license What can it do? ¶ Area Highlights Resolution Cooper–Nathans and Popovici formalisms; R0 prefactor and 4×4 RMS / RM matrices in Q–E and HKL–E frames Convolution fitting Fit S(Q,ω) model parameters against measured scans with the resolution convolved in ( FitConv , UltraFastFitConv ) Crystallography Lattice metrics, UB orientation matrix, 230 space groups, nuclear/magnetic structure factors, built-in databases GUIs Resolution calculator, Q-scan fit, E-scan fit — launched from one console command Where to start ¶ Installation — install and verify. Quick start — first resolution calculation in a few lines. CLI reference — the inspy-conv command. User guide: Energy · Crystallography · Resolution · Fitting · GUIs Developer guide: Architecture · Development Minimal example ¶ import inspy tas = inspy.TripleAxisSpectr(efixed=14.7) tas.sample = inspy.Sample(3, 4, 5, 90, 90, 90) tas.CalcResMatHKL([2, 0, 0, 0]) # stores tas.R0, tas.RMS, tas.RM print(tas.R0)

docs.text: Architecture ¶ Layout ¶ inspy-conv/ ├── pyproject.toml # setuptools build, deps, console script, package data ├── README.md # project overview (points here) ├── mkdocs.yml # this documentation site ├── docs/ # documentation sources (Markdown) ├── src/inspy/ # the package (import name: inspy) │ ├── __main__.py # CLI dispatch (lazy per-mode imports) │ ├── constants.py # physical constants + JSON database loaders │ ├── energy.py # Energy conversions (from neutronpy conventions) │ ├── crystal/ # lattice, sample, atoms, symmetry, structure factors │ ├── instrument/ # TAS/TOF spectrometers, mono/ana, projection tools │ ├── insfit/ # resolution-convolution fitters │ ├── gui/ # Qt dialogs + shared tools + ui/*.ui files │ └── database/*.json # packaged data files ├── tests/ # pytest suite + GUI scratch scripts └── ResLib3.4c/ # upstream MATLAB reference (not installed) Module dependency graph (simplified) ¶ constants │ ┌───────┴────────┐ energy crystal ◄──── database/*.json │ │ └───────┬────────┘ instrument ──────────► ResLib3.4c (algorithm reference) │ insfit │ gui ────────────────► lmfit, QtPy/PySide6 (fitting dialogs) │ __main__ (CLI) inspy/__init__ (public API) Rules of thumb visible in the code: Lower layers never import upper layers. crystal does not know about instrument ; insfit does not know about gui . GUI modules are leaves. Only __main__ (or the user) imports them. Databases load lazily through constants.py on first use. Lazy import design ¶ Two mechanisms keep import inspy cheap and robust: inspy/gui/__init__.py imports nothing eagerly. The three GUI modules (and their lmfit /Qt dependencies) are pulled in by __main__ 's PROGRAMS dispatch only when the corresponding CLI flag is selected. Importing a concrete module directly ( from inspy.gui.gui_convfit_qscan_uf import main ) still works — Python imports submodules on demand. (Older docs suggested from inspy.gui import main_qscan ; that re-export was removed in 0.3.x — use the concrete module path above.) inspy.main uses a PEP 562 module __getattr__ . The attribute is resolved on first access: inspy.main() imports gui.main_gui at call time. A missing Qt stack therefore surfaces exactly when the GUI is requested (with the historical warning), not at import inspy . # inspy/__init__.py (simplified) def __getattr__(name): if name == 'main': try: from .gui.main_gui import main except ImportError: warnings.warn('QtPy not found, cannot run Resolution GUI.') raise return main raise AttributeError(name) The resolution engine ¶ instrument/tas_spectr.py implements the ResLib 3.4c port: _StandardSystem() — build the sample/reciprocal frames from Sample . CalcResMatQ(Q, W) — Cooper–Nathans or Popovici in the Q frame → R0 , RM . CalcResMatHKL(hkle) — rotate into the (H,K,L,E) frame → self.R0/RMS/RM (stored on the instance; returns None ). ResConv(...) — convolve an S(Q,ω) model on a quadrature grid. Plot methods render the ellipses/ellipsoids from the same matrices. insfit calls ResConv repeatedly through least_squares ( method='trf' ), with UltraFastFitConv adding caching and precomputation. Packaging ¶ Build backend: setuptools>=77 ( pyproject.toml ). Package discovery: src/ layout ( [tool.setuptools.packages.find] ). Package data: database/*.json , gui/ui/*.ui (explicitly declared). Console script: inspy-conv = "inspy.__main__:main" . Optional dev extra: .[dev] → pytest, flake8. File encodings ¶ Most files: UTF-8, LF line endings, no BOM. tas_spectr.py in particular is LF-only with no trailing newline — keep edits raw-text to avoid introducing CRLF (the MATLAB port was converted wholesale).

docs.text: CLI reference ¶ Installing the package adds one console command, inspy-conv (defined in pyproject.toml as inspy.__main__:main ). Synopsis ¶ inspy-conv [-h] [-rescalc | -escan | -qscan] Options ¶ Flag Effect (none) Launch the resolution calculation GUI (default) -rescalc Same as default — resolution calculation GUI -escan Launch the energy-scan convolution-fit GUI ( gui_convfit_escan_uf ) -qscan Launch the Q-scan convolution-fit GUI ( gui_convfit_qscan_uf ) -h , --help Show usage and exit The three mode flags are mutually exclusive (argparse mutually-exclusive group); combining them is an error. Examples ¶ inspy-conv # resolution calculator inspy-conv -escan # E-scan fitting inspy-conv -qscan # Q-scan fitting python -m inspy -qscan # equivalent module form Behaviour ¶ On start the command prints Running inspy in the <mode> mode. and then runs the selected GUI's main() . The selected GUI module is imported lazily , only after the flag is parsed. If the import fails (missing Qt binding, missing lmfit , …), the command prints Error: cannot start <mode> (<description>): <detail> to stderr and exits with status 1 — other modes are unaffected. A missing dependency therefore affects only the mode that needs it; see Installation → Lazy imports . Programmatic equivalent ¶ from inspy.__main__ import main main([]) # resolution calculator main(['-escan']) # energy-scan GUI main(['-qscan']) # Q-scan GUI GUI modules can also be started directly (the package __init__ deliberately re-exports nothing GUI-related — import the concrete module): import inspy inspy.main() # resolution calculator (lazy attribute) from inspy.gui.gui_convfit_qscan_uf import main main() # Q-scan GUI

docs.text: Crystallography ¶ All classes below are importable from inspy directly or from inspy.crystal . from inspy.crystal import (Lattice, Sample, Atom, MagneticAtom, Material, SpaceGroup, NuclearStructureFactor, MagneticFormFactor, MagneticStructureFactor) Units Lattice constants are in Å , angles ( alpha , beta , gamma ) in degrees . Radian variants are derived internally where needed. Lattice ¶ Defined by six parameters; provides metric tensors, reciprocal lattice, d-spacing, and volume. lat = Lattice(5.0, 5.0, 5.0, 90, 90, 90) lat.volume # 125.0 Å³ lat.get_d_spacing([1, 0, 0]) # 5.0 Å lat.get_q([1, 0, 0]) # |Q| = 2π/d for that reflection lat.G, lat.Gstar # metric tensors (direct / reciprocal) lat.Bmatrix # Cartesian basis matrix (B.T @ B = Gstar) lat.get_two_theta([1, 1, 1], wavelength=1.5) # Bragg angle (deg) Useful properties: abc , abg (degrees), abg_rad , astar/bstar/cstar , alphastar/betastar/gammastar , lattice_type (auto-classified: triclinic/monoclinic/orthorhombic/…). Sample ¶ Sample extends Lattice with the physical/orientational properties needed by a spectrometer calculation: orientation vectors u , v , mosaic spread, and sample shape. s = Sample(3, 4, 5, 90, 90, 90, u=[1, 0, 0], v=[0, 1, 0], mosaic=30, vmosaic=30, width=20, height=20, depth=0.2) s.Umatrix # orientation matrix (u, v) s.UBmatrix # full UB matrix — hkl -> Q in the lab frame s.get_phi(Q) # rotation phi aligning Q into the scattering plane Sample is what TripleAxisSpectr.sample expects. Atom / MagneticAtom ¶ atom = Atom('Mn', pos=[0, 0, 0], occupancy=1.0, Uiso=0.005) atom.b # coherent scattering length (from scattering_lengths.json) atom.mass # atomic mass (from periodic_table.json) Atom looks up coherent/incoherent scattering lengths, cross sections, mass, and number density from the bundled databases. MagneticAtom adds magnetic moment / form-factor lookup. Material ¶ Material = Sample + structure factors, built from a dictionary-based description of a crystal: crystal = { 'name': 'MnO', 'lattice': {'abc': [4.445, 4.445, 4.445], 'abg': [90, 90, 90]}, 'space_group': 'Fm-3m', 'massNorm': False, 'formulaUnits': 1, # optional, default 1 'composition': [ {'ion': 'Mn', 'pos': [0, 0, 0], 'occupancy': 1.0}, {'ion': 'O', 'pos': [0.5, 0.5, 0.5], 'occupancy': 1.0}, ], } mat = Material(crystal) mat.calc_nuc_str_fac([1, 1, 1]) # nuclear structure factor Notes on the dictionary keys: 'lattice' is a nested dict with 'abc' (Å) and 'abg' (degrees) lists. 'massNorm' is read whenever 'space_group' is present — include it. Per-composition 'occupancy' , 'Uiso' , 'Uaniso' default to 1 / 0 / zeros. With a space group, each listed site is expanded through symmetrize_position to the full set of equivalent positions. It inherits from Sample , NuclearStructureFactor , and MagneticStructureFactor . SpaceGroup ¶ Any of the 230 groups, addressed by international symbol, Hermann–Mauguin symbol, or number: sg = SpaceGroup('Fm-3m') # or SpaceGroup(225), SpaceGroup('P 21 21 21') sg.group_number sg.symmetry_operations # list of operations sg.symmetrize_position([0, 0, 0]) # symmetry-equivalent positions Backed by database/symmetry.json . Structure factors ¶ Class / method Purpose NuclearStructureFactor.calc_nuc_str_fac(hkl) Nuclear structure factor F(hkl) with Debye–Waller factors MagneticFormFactor(ion) Magnetic form-factor coefficients (j0, j2, j4) for an ion, from magnetic_form_factors.json MagneticStructureFactor Magnetic structure factor (partially implemented — magnetic interaction vector components exist; full polarization analysis is stubbed) Databases ¶ Four JSON files ship with the package and are loaded on demand: File Loader Contents periodic_table.json periodic_table() mass, Z, density scattering_lengths.json scattering_lengths() coherent/incoherent b, cross sections magnetic_form_factors.json magnetic_ion_j() j0, j2, j4 coefficients symmetry.json symmetry() the 230 space groups Loader functions live in inspy.constants .

docs.text: Development ¶ Setup ¶ git clone https://github.com/gcdengansto/inspy-conv cd inspy-conv python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate # or .venv\Scripts\activate on Windows pip install -e ".[dev]" Run the tests: pytest tests/ The suite is small ( test_tas.py , test_mc.py , inspy_test.py ) — it exercises the TAS engine and conversions, not the GUIs. The files tests/main_gui.py , tests/res_3D_plot.py are scratch scripts for manual GUI runs, not pytest modules. Conventions ¶ Fix markers ¶ Every behavioural fix since 2026-10-10 carries a marker comment: #20261010: <tag> Fix: <what was wrong and what changed> Tags used so far: L1 … L11 (low-priority cleanups), M1 … M11 (medium), H1 (high), Bug #2.x (ResLib-port divergences), §n.m (review-report items). When editing a marked block, keep the marker with the code it describes. Comment style ¶ Corrections to the ported MATLAB comments use #20261010: markers with the reasoning inline (why, not just what). Known-but-unfixed issues are marked KNOWN ISSUE (...) with a pointer to the review report section. Original-author credit: where a file is adapted from ResLib 3.4c or neutronpy, the header says so — do not remove attribution. Line references ¶ Review comments cite file.py:NNN . Insertions inside cited ranges shift the numbers: prefer line-neutral edits (fold a note into an existing comment line) or update the inbound references in the same pass. Line endings ¶ Keep files LF . tas_spectr.py is LF-only, no BOM, no trailing newline. Review reports ¶ The repository root carries the static-review trail (kept as historical records, not part of the package): File Contents proj_potential_problems.md Initial problem inventory proj_review_output.md First full static review proj_review_output_v2.md Second pass + fixes proj_review_output_v3.md Findings + §9 fix log (code fixes) proj_review_comments_v4.md Comment/docstring audit + status notes + recommended actions Fix work follows: read the report section → verify against the current tree → apply → append a Status note under the section. Documentation ¶ Sources live in docs/ (Markdown, MkDocs-compatible): pip install mkdocs mkdocs serve # live preview at http://127.0.0.1:8000 mkdocs build # static site/ folder (deploy anywhere) To publish online, push mkdocs build output to GitHub Pages ( mkdocs gh-deploy ) or any static host. The nav is defined in mkdocs.yml — add new pages there. When you change an API: Update the docstring in the source. Update the matching page in docs/ . Check the examples in README.md . Known limitations (tracked, not forgotten) ¶ Item Where documented bounds not forwarded to least_squares fitconv.py fitwithconv note cache_size reserved but unused uffitconv.py note Magnetic structure factor partially stubbed crystal/structure_factors.py TimeOfFlightSpectr stub-level instrument/tof_spectr.py Dead 2.6/3.3 version check inspy/__init__.py note Demo S(Q,ω) models are examples, not physics-complete gui/tools.py Code-level review status lives in proj_review_comments_v4.md §6/§7.

docs.text: Energy ¶ inspy.Energy converts between the common units of a neutron's state. Adapted from neutronpy conventions. Constructor ¶ Energy(energy=None, wavelength=None, velocity=None, wavevector=None, temperature=None, frequency=None) Pass exactly one quantity; the others are derived from it. Keyword Unit Meaning energy meV Neutron energy E wavelength Å de Broglie wavelength λ wavevector 1/Å k = 2π/λ velocity m/s Group velocity v temperature K Equivalent temperature (E = k_B·T) frequency THz E = ħ·ω Properties ¶ After construction, all of energy , wavelength , wavevector , velocity , temperature , frequency are available as attributes (read-only conversions). Examples ¶ from inspy import Energy e = Energy(energy=14.7) print(e.wavelength) # ~2.3739 Å print(e.wavevector) # ~2.6473 1/Å w = Energy(wavelength=2.5) print(w.energy) # ~13.06 meV # equality compares energies (within 1e-6 meV) Energy(energy=14.7) == Energy(energy=14.7) # True Typical use in resolution work ¶ The fixed energy of the spectrometer is specified in meV: tas = inspy.TripleAxisSpectr(efixed=14.7) and the Bose factor used by demo S(Q,ω) models converts energies to temperature units internally ( W / (k_B·T) ).

docs.text: Convolution fitting ¶ Measured scan = S(Q,ω) convolved with the instrument resolution. Instead of fitting analytic peak shapes, inspy-conv fits the model by numerically convolving it at every iteration. The pieces ¶ Piece Role TripleAxisSpectr Resolution engine (see Resolution ) sqw(H, K, L, W, p) S(Q,ω) model — a callable returning intensity on the scan grid pref(H, K, L, W, EXP, p) Prefactor model — polarization, form factor, overall scale FitConv / UltraFastFitConv Optimiser driving the loop Demo models ship in inspy.gui.tools : SqwDemo — two-peak E-scan model (Lorentzians in W, Bose factor, ratio p[2] multiplies peak 1 ) — used by the E-scan GUI . SqwQScanTwoPeaks — two Gaussians in Q, width p[3] / p[4] are the FWHM in Q , ratio p[2] multiplies peak 2 — used by the Q-scan GUI . PrefDemoFF — polarization ⊗ magnetic form factor ⊗ overall scale p[5] . Note the ratio convention The two demo models differ: SqwDemo applies the intensity ratio to peak 1, SqwQScanTwoPeaks applies it to peak 2. See GUIs → printed output . FitConv ¶ from inspy import FitConv fitter = FitConv(exp=tas, sqw=sqw_func, prefactor=pref_func, hkle=hkle, Iobs=Iobs, dIobs=dIobs, param=param, paramfixed=param_fixed_mask) fitter.fitwithconv(...) Optimiser: scipy.optimize.least_squares with method='trf' (Trust-Region Reflective; lm would be Levenberg–Marquardt). param is a flat numpy array of model parameters; paramfixed a 0/1 mask. Bounds: see the note in the source — bounds are not currently forwarded to least_squares (known limitation, documented at the call site). UltraFastFitConv ¶ from inspy import UltraFastFitConv fitter = UltraFastFitConv(tas, sqw_func, pref_func, hkle, Iobs, dIobs, cache_size=128, precompute_data=True) result = fitter.fit_ultrafast(param_initial, param_fixed_mask) Optimisations over FitConv : Pre-computed data — hkle grids and static factors are prepared once. LRU caching of repeated resolution evaluations ( cache_size ; the value is currently reserved — see source note). Adaptive Jacobian steps — central differences with parameter-aware step sizes (two ResConv calls per free parameter). Both classes follow the ResLib FitConv / FitConvSMA structure. Writing your own model ¶ def my_sqw(H, K, L, W, p): """Gaussian in H centred at p[0], width p[1], scale p[2].""" import numpy as np return p[2] * np.exp(-(H - p[0])**2 / (2 * p[1]**2)) def my_pref(H, K, L, W, EXP, p): """Flat prefactor.""" return np.full_like(np.asarray(W, dtype=float), 1.0) Conventions the fitter expects: The model must broadcast over the scan grid (same shape as hkle slices). Temperature/energy conversions inside Bose factors should use meV ( W / (k_B T) with k_B = 0.08617 meV/K, as in the demo models). Fitting from the GUI ¶ The Q-scan and E-scan GUIs wrap the fitters with data loading, plotting, and parameter tables — see GUIs .

docs.text: GUIs ¶ Three Qt (PySide6 via QtPy) interfaces ship with the package. They are imported lazily — see Installation . Launching ¶ inspy-conv # resolution calculator (default) inspy-conv -escan # energy-scan fit inspy-conv -qscan # Q-scan fit or from Python: import inspy inspy.main() # resolution calculator from inspy.gui import gui_convfit_escan_uf, gui_convfit_qscan_uf gui_convfit_escan_uf.main() # E-scan fit gui_convfit_qscan_uf.main() # Q-scan fit Each module also has a MainWindow class if you want to embed it. 1. Resolution calculator — main_gui.py ¶ The default mode. Three linked resolution panels ( QxQy, QxE, QyE ) with the full instrument parameter set (collimation, arms, mono/ana, sample, energy) editable in side docks. Recalculates CalcResMatHKL + ResolutionPlotProj interactively. UI definition: src/inspy/gui/ui/resolution.ui (Qt Designer). 2. Q-scan fit — gui_convfit_qscan_uf.py ¶ Fit a constant-Q scan (intensity vs QH/QK/QL) with the resolution convolved in. Model: SqwQScanTwoPeaks — two Gaussians in Q (widths p[3] , p[4] are FWHM in Q ), ratio p[2] scales peak 2 , p[5] overall scale (via PrefDemoFF ). Data: load a text/table file, select the H K L W Iobs dIobs columns. Uses UltraFastFitConv with lmfit for parameter handling/reporting. 3. E-scan fit — gui_convfit_escan_uf.py ¶ Fit a constant-E scan (intensity vs energy transfer). Model: SqwDemo — two Lorentzians in W with Bose factor (Γ₁ = p[3] , Γ₂ = p[4] are HWHM ), ratio p[2] scales peak 1 . Same data-loading and fitting flow as the Q-scan GUI. Printed output ¶ After a fit both fitting dialogs print a parameter table. Conventions: Label Meaning QH1/QH2 (or EN1/EN2 for E-scan) peak centres, error Int1/Int2 peak integrals — Int1 belongs to peak 1 (under the first centre label), Int2 to peak 2 FWHM1/FWHM2 (Q-scan) Gaussian FWHM in Q — equals the model width p[3] / p[4] HWHM1/HWHM2 (E-scan) Lorentzian HWHM — equals p[3] / p[4] ratio intensity-ratio parameter p[2] bg , temp background p[6] , temperature p[7] Fixed in the 2026-10 review The Q-scan dialog's widths were briefly mislabelled HWHM during the port; they are Gaussian FWHM and are printed as FWHM1/FWHM2 . Q-scan Int1/Int2 were swapped relative to the model (the ratio multiplies peak 2 there); they are now printed in peak order with first-order error propagation on Int2 = ratio·p5 . Qt / headless notes ¶ The GUIs need a working Qt binding ( PySide6 by default through QtPy ). On headless machines the calculation core ( TripleAxisSpectr , fitting classes) still works — only the GUIs refuse to start.

docs.text: Installation ¶ Requirements ¶ Python ≥ 3.8 Core dependencies (installed automatically): numpy , scipy , matplotlib , pandas , lmfit , h5py , plotly GUI dependencies: QtPy + PySide6 (also in the default dependency list) From PyPI ¶ pip install inspy-conv Editable (development) install ¶ git clone https://github.com/gcdengansto/inspy-conv cd inspy-conv pip install -e . For running the test suite: pip install -e ".[dev]" # adds pytest, flake8 Verify the install ¶ import inspy print(inspy.__version__) # e.g. "0.3.3" en = inspy.Energy(energy=14.7) print(en.wavelength) # ~2.37 Å The console command should also be on PATH : inspy-conv -h Lazy imports and optional GUIs ¶ The package uses lazy loading : import inspy loads only the core scientific stack (constants, crystal, instrument, insfit) — no Qt, no GUI modules . inspy.main is resolved on first access (PEP 562 __getattr__ ), which then imports the resolution-calculation GUI. Each CLI mode imports its own GUI module only when its flag is selected, so a missing fit-dialog dependency (Qt backend, lmfit ) breaks only that mode — not import inspy and not the other modes. Practical consequence: on a headless/batch analysis machine you can install and use the calculation core without a working Qt stack, as long as you do not launch the GUIs. Troubleshooting ¶ Symptom Likely cause Fix inspy.main raises ImportError , warning QtPy not found... Qt bindings missing pip install PySide6 (or another QtPy-supported binding) -qscan / -escan fail with lmfit import error lmfit missing pip install lmfit pip install succeeds but import inspy fails Broken environment / path Reinstall with pip install --force-reinstall inspy-conv Package data ( database/*.json , gui/ui/*.ui ) missing Old install tooling Reinstall from PyPI or use an editable install; data files are declared in pyproject.toml Upgrading ¶ pip install --upgrade inspy-conv

docs.text: Quick start ¶ This walkthrough computes a resolution matrix and draws the resolution ellipsoid for a simple instrument. 1. Energy units ¶ import inspy en = inspy.Energy(energy=14.7) # meV print(en.wavelength) # Å print(en.wavevector) # 1/Å print(en.velocity) # m/s Energy accepts any one of energy , wavelength , wavevector , velocity , temperature , or frequency and converts to the rest — see Energy . 2. Define the sample ¶ sample = inspy.Sample( a=3.0, b=4.0, c=5.0, # lattice constants (Å) alpha=90, beta=90, gamma=90, # angles — in DEGREES u=[1, 0, 0], v=[0, 1, 0], # orientation vectors mosaic=30, vmosaic=30, # mosaic spread (arcmin) ) print(sample.UBmatrix) # UB orientation matrix Note All lattice angles throughout the package are in degrees . The reciprocal quantities ( abg_rad , etc.) are derived internally where radians are needed. 3. Configure the spectrometer ¶ from inspy.instrument import TripleAxisSpectr, Mono, Ana mono = Mono(tau='PG(002)', mosaic=30, vmosaic=30, height=20, width=20, depth=0.2, rh=150, rv=150, direct=-1) ana = Ana(tau='PG(002)', mosaic=30, vmosaic=30, height=20, width=20, depth=0.2, rh=150, rv=150, direct=-1, thickness=0.2, horifoc=-1) tas = TripleAxisSpectr( efixed=14.7, # fixed energy (meV) — fixed-Ef if infin=-1 (default) method=1, # 0 = Cooper-Nathans, 1 = Popovici (default) mono=mono, ana=ana, sample=sample, ) tas.hcol = [40, 40, 40, 120] # horizontal collimation (arcmin): L0,L1,L2,L3 tas.arms = [200, 100, 100, 200] # distances (cm) tau accepts a crystal name from the built-in table ( 'PG(002)' , 'Si(111)' , 'Ge(111)' , 'Cu(111)' , …) or a numeric value in Å⁻¹. 4. Calculate the resolution ¶ tas.CalcResMatHKL([2, 0, 0, 0]) # (H, K, L, E) tas.R0 # prefactor -> shape (N,) tas.RMS # 4x4 matrix (HKL-E) -> shape (N, 4, 4) tas.RM # 4x4 matrix (Q frame) -> shape (N, 4, 4) Important CalcResMatHKL returns None and stores the results on the instrument ( self.R0 , self.RMS , self.RM ). Earlier README revisions showed a tuple unpack — that was wrong. Batch calculation works by passing a (4, N) array: import numpy as np hkle = np.array([[2, 0, 0, 0], [2, 0, 0, 2], [3, 0, 0, 0]]) tas.CalcResMatHKL(hkle.T) # N = 3 points print(tas.RMS.shape) # (3, 4, 4) 5. Plot ¶ tas.ResolutionPlot(hkle=[2, 0, 0, 0]) # 4-panel plot tas.ResolutionPlotProj(qslice='QxQy', hkle=[2, 0, 0, 0]) # single panel tas.ResolutionPlot3D(hkle=[2, 0, 0, 0]) # 3D ellipsoid 6. Angles both ways ¶ tas.get_angles_and_Q([2, 0, 0, 0]) # HKL-E -> spectrometer angles tas.get_hkl_and_Q(M2, S1, S2, A2) # motor angles -> HKL-E Next steps ¶ Full configuration and theory: Resolution Fit a model to data: Convolution fitting Interactive use: GUIs

docs.text: Resolution calculation ¶ The core of the package is inspy.TripleAxisSpectr ( src/inspy/instrument/tas_spectr.py , ~2 900 lines) — a faithful Python port of MATLAB ResLib 3.4c by A. Zheludev. Theory in one page ¶ A triple-axis spectrometer measures a convolution of the sample cross section with the instrument resolution function. Near a point in (Q, E) the resolution is approximated as a 4-dimensional Gaussian characterised by: R₀ — a dimensionless prefactor (normalisation of the Gaussian), and RMS — the 4×4 inverse covariance matrix ("resolution matrix") in the measurement frame. Two formalisms are implemented, selectable per instrument via method : method Formalism Notes 0 Cooper–Nathans Analytic Gaussian approximation; older, simpler 1 Popovici (default) Improves Cooper–Nathans, closer to Monte-Carlo Both follow the classic chain: project source/beam-monitor/monochromator/sample/ analyzer/detector phasespaces through the spectrometer arms ( arms , hcol , vcol ), rotate into the sample frame, and (optionally) apply resolution smoothing ( Smooth ) or sample-shape correction. Key intermediate quantities: Symbol in code Meaning R0 Prefactor, shape (N,) RMS 4×4 matrix in the (H,K,L,E) frame, shape (N,4,4) RM 4×4 matrix in the Q frame (before HKL rotation), shape (N,4,4) self.method 0 = Cooper–Nathans, 1 = Popovici self.infin −1 fixed E_f, +1 fixed E_i (default −1) Instrument configuration ¶ from inspy.instrument import TripleAxisSpectr, Mono, Ana tas = TripleAxisSpectr( efixed=14.7, # fixed energy (meV) method=1, # Popovici (default) mono=mono, ana=ana, sample=sample, hcol=[40, 40, 40, 120], # arcmin: before mono, before sample, # before ana, after ana vcol=[120, 120, 120, 120], # vertical collimation (or default) ) tas.arms = [200, 100, 100, 200] # cm: L0 L1 L2 L3 (L1mon extra, optional) Sub-components can also be passed piecewise as keyword arguments ( mono_tau='PG(002)' , sample_a=3.0 , …); the constructor builds the components for you. Monochromator / Analyzer ¶ mono = Mono(tau='PG(002)', mosaic=30, vmosaic=30, height=20, width=20, depth=0.2, rh=150, rv=150, direct=-1) ana = Ana(tau='PG(002)', mosaic=30, vmosaic=30, ..., thickness=0.2, horifoc=-1) tau — crystal name from the built-in table ( get_tau ), or a numeric value. Table entries include PG(002), Si(111), Ge(111/220/311/511/533), Cu(111/002/220), … direct — −1/+1 focusing direction; rh , rv — horizontal/vertical focusing radii (cm). Main methods ¶ Method Description CalcResMatHKL(hkle) Resolution at (H,K,L,E); stores self.R0 , self.RMS , self.RM , returns None . Accepts (4,) or (4,N) . CalcResMatQ(Q, W) Same, in Q–E frame (internal entry point used by the HKL version) ResConv(sqw, pref, nargout, hkle, ...) docs.text: The core of the package is inspy.TripleAxisSpectr ( src/inspy/instrument/tas_spectr.py , ~2 900 lines) — a faithful Python port of MATLAB ResLib 3.4c by A. Zheludev.
docs.title: Resolution calculation

docs.text: A triple-axis spectrometer measures a convolution of the sample cross section with the instrument resolution function. Near a point in (Q, E) the resolution is approximated as a 4-dimensional Gaussian characterised by: R₀ — a dimensionless prefactor (normalisation of the Gaussian), and RMS — the 4×4 inverse covariance matrix ("resolution matrix") in the measurement frame. Two formalisms are implemented, selectable per instrument via method : method Formalism Notes 0 Cooper–Nathans Analytic Gaussian approximation; older, simpler 1 Popovici (default) Improves Cooper–Nathans, closer to Monte-Carlo Both follow the classic chain: project source/beam-monitor/monochromator/sample/ analyzer/detector phasespaces through the spectrometer arms ( arms , hcol , vcol ), rotate into the sample frame, and (optionally) apply resolution smoothing ( Smooth ) or sample-shape correction. Key intermediate quantities: Symbol in code Meaning R0 Prefactor, shape (N,) RMS 4×4 matrix in the (H,K,L,E) frame, shape (N,4,4) RM 4×4 matrix in the Q frame (before HKL rotation), shape (N,4,4) self.method 0 = Cooper–Nathans, 1 = Popovici self.infin −1 fixed E_f, +1 fixed E_i (default −1)
docs.title: Theory in one page

docs.text: from inspy.instrument import TripleAxisSpectr, Mono, Ana tas = TripleAxisSpectr( efixed=14.7, # fixed energy (meV) method=1, # Popovici (default) mono=mono, ana=ana, sample=sample, hcol=[40, 40, 40, 120], # arcmin: before mono, before sample, # before ana, after ana vcol=[120, 120, 120, 120], # vertical collimation (or default) ) tas.arms = [200, 100, 100, 200] # cm: L0 L1 L2 L3 (L1mon extra, optional) Sub-components can also be passed piecewise as keyword arguments ( mono_tau='PG(002)' , sample_a=3.0 , …); the constructor builds the components for you.
docs.title: Instrument configuration

docs.text: mono = Mono(tau='PG(002)', mosaic=30, vmosaic=30, height=20, width=20, depth=0.2, rh=150, rv=150, direct=-1) ana = Ana(tau='PG(002)', mosaic=30, vmosaic=30, ..., thickness=0.2, horifoc=-1) tau — crystal name from the built-in table ( get_tau ), or a numeric value. Table entries include PG(002), Si(111), Ge(111/220/311/511/533), Cu(111/002/220), … direct — −1/+1 focusing direction; rh , rv — horizontal/vertical focusing radii (cm).
